answers: Military families with special medical and educational needs face unique challenges because of their frequent moves. To help assist these families, DOD provides services plans, which document the support a family member requires. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2017 included a provision for GAO to review the Services' EFMPs, including DOD's oversight of these programs. This report examines the extent to which (1) each Service provides family support and (2) the Services monitor and DOD evaluates assignment coordination and family support. GAO analyzed DOD and Service-specific EFMP guidance and documents; analyzed fiscal year 2016 EFMP data (the most recent available); visited seven military installations, selected for their large numbers of military-connected students; and interviewed officials responsible for implementing each Service's EFMP, as well as officials in OSN that administer DOD's EFM policy. The support provided to families with special needs through the Department of Defense's (DOD) Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP) varies widely for each branch of Military Service. Federal law requires DOD's Office of Special Needs (OSN) to develop a uniform policy that includes requirements for (1) developing and updating a services plan for each family with special needs and (2) resources, such as staffing, to ensure an appropriate number of family support providers. OSN has developed such a policy, but DOD relies on each Service to determine its compliance with the policy. However, Army and Navy officials said they have not received feedback from OSN about the extent to which their Service-specific guidance complies. Federal internal control standards call for developing clear policies to achieve agency goals. In addition, DOD's most recent annual reports to Congress do not indicate the extent to which each Service provides services plans or allocates sufficient resources for family support providers. According to GAO's analysis, the Military Services have developed relatively few services plans, and there is wide variation in the number of family support providers employed, which raises questions about potential gaps in services for families with special needs (see table). Each Service uses various mechanisms to monitor how servicemembers are assigned to installations (assignment coordination) and obtain family support, but DOD has not established common performance measures to assess these activities. DOD has taken steps to better support families with special needs, according to the DOD officials GAO interviewed. For example, DOD established a working group to identify gaps in services. However, OSN officials said that DOD lacks common performance measures for assignment coordination and family support because the Services have not reached consensus on what those measures should be. In addition, OSN does not have a process to systematically evaluate the results of the Services' monitoring activities. Federal internal control standards call for assessing performance over time and evaluating the results of monitoring activities. Without establishing common performance measures and assessing monitoring activities, DOD will be unable to fully determine the effect of its efforts to better support families with special needs and the adequacy of the Services' EFMPs as required by federal law. GAO makes a total of three recommendations to DOD. DOD should assess and report to Congress on the extent to which each Service provides sufficient family support personnel and services plans, develop common performance metrics for assignment coordination and family support, and evaluate the results of the Services' monitoring activities. DOD agreed with these recommendations and plans to develop performance metrics for assignment coordination and develop plans to evaluate the Services' monitoring activities.

**Summary of the Report on the Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP)**

The Department of Defense (DOD) manages the Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP) to support military families with special needs, ensuring they receive appropriate care and services as their servicemembers relocate. The EFMP is structured around three core components: identification and enrollment, assignment coordination, and family support. Each military service—Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Navy—has its own EFMP, with the Office of Special Needs (OSN) overseeing the program and working to standardize procedures across services.

Servicemembers and their families with special medical or educational needs are identified and enrolled by medical and educational personnel at installations. Once enrolled, families are supported through a range of services, including assistance with accessing medical and educational resources, legal support, and case management. The EFMP also includes the development of services plans (SPs) to document and track the support provided to each family, especially during relocations.

Despite these efforts, the report highlights significant variation in how the services implement the EFMP. For example, the frequency of contact with families, availability of legal assistance, and the development of services plans differ across services. The Air Force, Army, and Navy do not employ special education attorneys, while the Marine Corps does. Additionally, the number of services plans created is relatively low compared to the number of families enrolled, with some services citing resource constraints and lack of standardized forms as contributing factors.

The report also notes that while DOD requires each service to monitor and evaluate its EFMP, there is no common set of performance metrics to assess the effectiveness of these programs. This lack of standardization makes it difficult for DOD to fully determine the adequacy of support provided to families with special needs and to identify gaps in service delivery. Furthermore, the absence of a systematic process to evaluate the results of monitoring activities limits DOD’s ability to ensure consistent support across services and installations.

To address these challenges, the report recommends that DOD direct OSN to assess the extent to which each service is providing sufficient resources for family support providers and developing services plans. It also recommends the development of common performance metrics for assignment coordination and family support, as well as the implementation of a systematic process for evaluating the results of monitoring activities conducted by each service.

**Summary of the Report on the Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP)**

The Department of Defense (DOD) manages the Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP) to support military families with special needs, ensuring they receive appropriate care and services during frequent relocations. The EFMP is structured around three core components: identification and enrollment, assignment coordination, and family support. Each military service—Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Navy—has its own EFMP, with the Office of Special Needs (OSN) overseeing the program and working to standardize procedures across services.

Servicemembers and their families with special medical or educational needs are identified and enrolled by medical and educational personnel at installations. Once enrolled, families are supported through case management, services plans, and access to community resources. Assignment coordination involves considering the availability of necessary services at new locations before finalizing a servicemember’s assignment. Family support includes assistance in accessing services, navigating the system, and developing individualized services plans (SPs) that track progress and ensure continuity of care during relocations.

Despite DOD’s efforts to standardize EFMP procedures, significant variation exists among services in the level of support provided, the frequency of contact with families, and the availability of legal and educational assistance. For example, the Marine Corps requires quarterly contact with families, while the Army has no such requirement. Additionally, only the Marine Corps employs special education attorneys, and other services rely on alternative means to assist families with legal issues.

The development and maintenance of services plans (SPs) is a key requirement under the NDAA for Fiscal Year 2010, yet the number of SPs remains low compared to the number of enrolled families. Reasons cited include insufficient staffing, lack of standardized forms, and the perception that some families do not require such plans. DOD has not established common performance metrics to assess the effectiveness of EFMPs, making it difficult to evaluate service consistency and identify gaps in support.

OSN has initiated efforts to standardize procedures and improve oversight, including the development of new forms and customer satisfaction surveys. However, without common performance measures, DOD cannot fully determine whether its long-term goals for EFMP are being met. The report recommends that DOD develop common performance metrics, assess resource adequacy across services, and implement a systematic process for evaluating monitoring activities.

Overall, while the EFMP provides essential support to military families with special needs, inconsistencies in service delivery and limited oversight highlight the need for greater standardization and improved performance measurement
